knowledge_points.label: Multimodality means converting every modality into tokens the Transformer can consume
knowledge_points.statement: Because Transformers work and Transformers consume sequences of tokens (discrete or continuous, each roughly a semantic unit), building a multimodal model reduces to two questions: how to turn non-text inputs (images, audio) into tokens for understanding, and how to produce non-text outputs from tokens for generation; text already needed this step (tokenization) and non-text modalities make it harder.

anchors.quote: Transformers work really well. So we gotta use them. ... Transformers speak tokens (discrete or continuous), where a token represents some ~semantic unit of information. ... Therefore, we must convert everything into tokens.
Note: we had to do this with text (recall the tokenization lecture). ... For non-text modalities, this is more challenging
Ultimate goal: **omni model** ... Input any combination of modalities (understanding) ... Output any combination of modalities (generation)
How do we input non-text data (e.g., understand images)? ... How do we output non-text data (e.g., generate audio)?
Fundamental challenge: how to encode non-text modalities? ... Comprehension and generation might demand different things (semantics versus finer-grained details)

And if you think about a North Star of where we want to be is what people call omni model, which is ability to take any combination of these modalities and output any combination of any of these modalities.

Well, this is a weird way to motivate this, but the reality is that transformers work really well. ... And despite the best efforts of people to try other things, those are across all of these modalities still at scale the best thing we have.

So they have this property that they speak tokens. ... You can think about these as embedding of tokens. ... And the key thing is that a token should represent some semantic unit of information. ... Whereas, for example, a pixel is certainly not meaningful by itself.
Now, notice that we've already had to do this even with text. ... Now, for non-text modalities, we have to scratch our heads a lot more and figure out what is the equivalent of the BP tokenizer
OK, so you have to answer two questions here. ... And then how do you generate them out? ... And this lecture will mostly focus on question number one.

misconceptions.belief: A multimodal token must be a discrete vocabulary index, like a word piece.
misconceptions.why_wrong: L17 says tokens may be 'discrete or continuous'; CLIP/SigLIP-based VLMs (L271) hand the LM continuous vectors that never pass through a vocabulary. Only Chameleon (L274) discretizes.

misconceptions.belief: Once images can be understood, generating images is the same problem solved in reverse.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The lecture lists input and output as separate questions (L23-L24) and says comprehension and generation 'might demand different things (semantics versus finer-grained details)' (L43); continuous-encoder VLMs 'can't generate images' (L272).

predict.q: A VLM feeds an image to its language model through a CLIP encoder. Which of these describes what the language model receives for the image?
choices: a sequence of continuous vectors that bypass the vocabulary embedding table
a sequence of integer ids drawn from an enlarged vocabulary
a single pooled vector prepended to the text
predict.answer: a sequence of continuous vectors that bypass the vocabulary embedding table
predict.why: Tokens can be 'discrete or continuous' (L17); the CLIP/SigLIP route encodes the image and injects the encodings into the LM (L271) via a projection into embedding space (L139). Integer ids are the Chameleon route (L274).

predict.distractor_from: integer ids: 'a multimodal token must be a discrete vocabulary index'; single pooled vector: conflating the CLIP classification embedding (L82) with the per-patch grid used by VLMs (L154)

transfer.q: A team has a strong text-only Transformer and wants it to both transcribe and synthesize speech. Using the lecture's framing, name the two separate design questions they must answer, and say which of the two the lecture says demands finer-grained detail.
transfer.answer: (1) How to turn audio input into tokens the Transformer can consume (understanding); (2) how to turn the Transformer's output into audio (generation). Generation is the one that demands finer-grained detail; comprehension needs semantics.
transfer.why: L23-L24 pose input and output as two questions; L43 says comprehension and generation 'might demand different things (semantics versus finer-grained details)'.
transfer.varies: modality: audio instead of the lecture's images (Barnett-Ceci modality dimension)
transfer.invariant: the Transformer only consumes and emits tokens, so each direction needs its own conversion

knowledge_points.label: CLIP: symmetric in-batch ranking of aligned (image, text) pairs
knowledge_points.statement: CLIP encodes a batch of N (image, text) pairs with separate encoders and trains both so that each image scores its own caption above the other N-1 captions and each caption scores its own image above the other N-1 images (a multiclass classification over the batch in both directions); this is far more compute-efficient than predicting the caption text from the image, but it needs large batches and a softmax over the whole batch.

anchors.quote: Get a batch of (image, text) examples (e.g., 32768) ... Encode each image and each text ... For each image, prefer its aligned text over other texts ... For each text, prefer its aligned image over other images
Alternative: predict text from images directly ... Much less compute efficient compared to CLIP-style ranking
Technical: requires large batch sizes, softmax operation over full batch
CLIP: multiclass classification for (text, image) versus (text, image') for all image'
Computer vision models were trained on annotated images. ... Question: is it possible to leverage the much larger amount of (image, caption) pairs?

anchors.ref: CLIP paper, Figure 1 / Figure 3 (contrastive pretraining and numpy pseudocode, shown at L54 and L61)

anchors.quote: And so the researchers at OpenAI were wondering, is it possible to leverage the large amount of image and textual captions out there? ... So what was the equivalent of that for images?

So let's say I give you 32,000 of these. ... So I1 is aligned with T1. ... So I want this alignment, the dot product between these two embeddings to be much larger than the dot product between I1 and all the other texts, OK.

And conversely, I also want for this text to say that this dot product is larger than the dot product between T1 and all the other images. ... there's basically 2 times N different softmax classification problems.

You normalize and you take this dot stop product with some temperature. ... And then you compute the cross entropy, OK. ... So it's basically a multi-class classification problem, where the examples are structured in this m by n matrix form.

they also try this alternative where instead of doing this ranking, they can predict a text from the images. ... Actually modeling the exact token sequences of the caption isn't so important for getting the rough representation of the image.

One technical downside of CLIP is that it does require large batch sizes, like 30,000. ... If you have a batch size of 1, clearly, it doesn't work, or even 10, it doesn't work. ... And furthermore, the softmax operation operates over the full batch. ... So it's not really very decomposable.

provenance.filtering_note: The loss itself is never written in text: clip-code.png (L61) is the paper's numpy pseudocode (cross-entropy over the N x N logit matrix along rows and along columns, averaged) and clip.png (L54) is the paper's overview figure; both are recorded as shown. '32768' at L57 is given as an example batch size. The efficiency ablation (L88-L90) is a figure (clip-efficiency.png) whose curves are not restated; the lecture's one-line reading is 'much less compute efficient'. The temperature parameter and the learned projection to the joint space are in the paper only. Correction (7:43): the note says the temperature parameter is in the paper only. Reading clip-code.png aloud he names it: 'You normalize and you take this dot ... product with some temperature'; the learned projection to the joint space is still not mentioned. Spoken evidence: the objective is '2 times N different softmax classification problems' (7:18); the ablation (L88-L90) is read aloud: predicting the caption text, 'if you use a stronger model, it actually does worse or at least is less efficient' than bag-of-words or the contrastive ranking, because 'modeling the exact token sequences of the caption isn't so important for getting the rough representation of the image' (20:12-21:24; he defers the point to the summary's understanding-versus-generation asymmetry, 1:15:39); why large batches: 'a batch size of 1 ... or even 10, it doesn't work', and the full-batch softmax is 'not really very decomposable', unlike LM training where sequences are independent until the final aggregation (22:01-22:37). '32,000' (6:05) and '30,000' (22:01) round L57's 32768. Q&A (18:43-19:23): other dog captions in the same batch act as false negatives; that is tolerated because 'on average, it's unlikely that there's always going to be a dog'.

prerequisites.note: CLIP is the lecture's first answer to 'how do we input non-text data' (L23).

misconceptions.belief: CLIP learns to generate or predict the caption of an image.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Predicting text from images is the alternative the paper ablated and found 'much less compute efficient' (L88-L89); CLIP only ranks the aligned caption above the other captions in the batch (L59-L60).

misconceptions.belief: The batch size in contrastive training is just a throughput knob, as in language modeling.
misconceptions.why_wrong: In CLIP the batch is the set of negatives: each image is classified against the other N-1 texts (L102), so the softmax runs over the full batch and the objective itself needs a large batch (L95).

predict.q: You train CLIP with a batch of 8 (image, text) pairs instead of 32768, keeping everything else fixed. How many wrong captions does each image have to be ranked against in one step?
predict.why: Each image prefers its aligned text over the other texts in the batch (L59); the negatives are the other N-1 = 7 captions, which is why the objective 'requires large batch sizes' (L95): with 8 the ranking problem is trivially easy.
predict.targets_misconception: The batch size in contrastive training is just a throughput knob, as in language modeling.

transfer.q: A team has 50M (product photo, audio jingle) pairs and wants an audio encoder whose embeddings can be searched by image. Say how the CLIP recipe applies: what plays the role of the text encoder, what each batch element is compared against, and why they should not instead train a model to generate the jingle from the photo.
transfer.answer: An audio encoder replaces the text encoder; in a batch of N pairs each photo is scored against all N jingles and each jingle against all N photos, with the aligned pair ranked first in both directions; generating the jingle directly would be the much less compute-efficient route the CLIP ablation rejected.
transfer.why: The method is modality-agnostic: encode each side, prefer the aligned partner over the other N-1 (L58-L60); the predict-the-other-side alternative was 'much less compute efficient' (L88-L89).
transfer.varies: modality of the second encoder: audio instead of text (modality dimension)
transfer.invariant: two encoders, symmetric in-batch ranking with the batch as the negative set

check.q: After CLIP training, you hold a new photo and its trained image and text encoders. Which of these can CLIP do with them directly, with no further training?
choices: score a list of candidate captions against the photo
write a new caption for the photo, one word at a time
decode the photo back from its embedding vector
check.answer: score a list of candidate captions against the photo
check.why: L57-L60 and L102: CLIP is trained to rank each image's aligned text above the other texts in the batch (a classification over candidates), not to generate text. The lecture notes that predicting text from images directly is much less compute-efficient (L88-L89). It has no image decoder either.
check.varies: asks what the trained model can do instead of how to adapt the recipe to audio
check.invariant: CLIP learns to rank aligned pairs above the other candidates; it does not generate
check.targets_misconception: CLIP learns to generate or predict the caption of an image.
distractor_from: 'write a new caption for the photo, one word at a time' <- misconception: 'CLIP learns to generate or predict the caption of an image.'
'decode the photo back from its embedding vector' <- plausible: treats a contrastive encoder as an autoencoder

retrieval.q: State the two symmetric preferences CLIP's objective enforces inside a batch.
retrieval.answer: Each image prefers its aligned text over the other texts; each text prefers its aligned image over the other images.

retrieval.q: What alternative objective did CLIP ablate, and what was the verdict?
retrieval.answer: Predicting the text from the image directly; much less compute efficient than contrastive ranking.

retrieval.q: Which technical requirement of CLIP does the lecture's summary flag?
retrieval.answer: Large batch sizes, with a softmax over the full batch.

prompts.self_explain: Why would ranking the right caption among N wrong ones be a cheaper learning signal than producing the caption word by word?

presentations.notice: listen for: each image must outscore every other caption and each caption every other image: 2N softmax classifications

Each row of the matrix is one softmax over the N captions, so image 1 is ranked against N − 1 wrong captions (the count in the readout), and the columns add N more softmaxes. Keep the cosines fixed and raise N: CLIP's probability for the same matched pair falls, because every extra caption adds to the denominator.

knowledge_points.label: CLIP preprocessing: resize and center-crop to 336, then 14x14 patches as tokens
knowledge_points.statement: CLIP forces every image to a fixed 336x336 input by bicubically resizing the shorter side to 336 and center-cropping, then its best vision encoder, ViT-L/14@336px, cuts that into 14x14-pixel patches, so every image becomes (336/14)^2 = 576 patch tokens of 14*14*3 = 588 raw values each (this thread's arithmetic); attention pooling with a global-average query summarises them, and the text side is a 63M-parameter GPT-2-style Transformer whose [EOS] activation is the text embedding.

anchors.quote: Images come in all resolutions (arbitrary W x H) ... Resize using bicubic interpolation so shorter side is 336 pixels ... Center crop (cuts off borders to get 336 x 336)
Attention pooling: do QKV with query = global average of activations ... Best model: ViT-L/14@336px (L = large, 14x14 patches, 3 channels, trained on 336x336 resolution images)
GPT-2 Transformer (63M parameters, 12 layers) ... Encode [BOS] ... [EOS], return [EOS] activation at highest layer
Experimented with ResNet-50 and Vision Transformers

anchors.ref: ViT architecture figure (vit.png, shown at L76)

anchors.quote: So images come in all sorts of resolutions. ... And one thing that you learn about neural nets is that they don't like things to be dynamic. ... They want things to be fixed size.

they resize the image so that the shorter side is 336 or whatever target size. ... And then they center crop to get a square. ... So usually, the object is in the middle and you're just trimming off some background.

So you take an image and you break it up into these patches. ... I think the original paper was 16 by 16 and the CLIP used 14 by 14. ... You add the positional embeddings just like you would if you were training a language model, and then you just put it through a standard transformer.

You can average all these vectors. ... But they thought it was better to do attention pooling, which means that you take the global average of all the activations, but then you also do another round of attention with that query against the key and values of each position.

And the CLIP paper found that the best model is what is called VIT-L/14. ... I think it has 24 layers or so. ... Actually, they trained on a lower res I guess for speed because high resolution images take longer. ... And then for the latter part of training, they train on higher res.
I think in this paper, they actually-- in the CLIP paper, I believe they tried some 2D version of this. ... So for classification, maybe it doesn't matter.
It's a GPT-2 style transformer since that was from the same group that developed GPT-2. ... And then they took EOS, the activation at the highest layer as the representation of that whole sequence.

provenance.filtering_note: The lecture never states the patch count; 576 = (336/14)^2 and 588 = 14*14*3 are this thread's arithmetic on L78's numbers. The ViT figure (L76) is the paper's; the linear patch-embedding, the class token and the ViT position embeddings are not mentioned in text. 'Attention pooling' (L77) is stated in one line: a single attention step whose query is the global average of the patch activations; the paper's exact pooling head differs between the ResNet and ViT variants, which the lecture does not distinguish. The 63M text encoder (L81) is the paper's base size; the lecture does not give the ViT-L parameter count. Center-cropping 'cuts off borders' (L72) is the information loss that AnyRes later fixes (L160). Spoken evidence: why a fixed size at all: neural nets 'don't like things to be dynamic' (9:57); why center-cropping was acceptable for CLIP: the authors had ImageNet classification in mind, where 'the object is in the middle and you're just trimming off some background' (10:35-10:48), and it was 'obviously for convenience' (10:27); 224 is named as another common target (10:20). Correction (13:31): the note says the ViT position embeddings are not mentioned; aloud: 'You add the positional embeddings just like you would if you were training a language model' (the linear patch embedding and class token are still not mentioned). Attention pooling is explained as one more attention step whose query is the global average (14:10-14:27), as in L77. ViT-L 'has 24 layers or so. Not quite sure' (14:54; ViT-L does have 24 layers, this thread's check). Training resolution: lower resolution for most of training, 336 'for the latter part' (15:13-15:23), consistent with the CLIP paper's extra epoch at 336 (this thread's reading of the paper). Q&A (15:40-16:13): 1D position ids reportedly work about as well as a 2D variant, 'for classification, maybe it doesn't matter'; he attributes the ablation to the CLIP paper with 'I believe', while the 1D-versus-2D comparison this thread knows of is in the ViT paper (Dosovitskiy et al., appendix), so the attribution is probably a slip (recollection, not checked); see also the flag on mrope-interleaved-axes. The text encoder is 'GPT-2 style ... from the same group' (16:30); its 63M parameters and 12 layers are not said aloud.

misconceptions.belief: A ViT sees the image at whatever resolution it was captured; higher-resolution photos give it more tokens.
misconceptions.why_wrong: CLIP first resizes and center-crops to 336x336 (L71-L72), so every image yields the same 576 patches regardless of its original W x H; extra pixels are discarded, not tokenised.

misconceptions.belief: '/14' in ViT-L/14 is the number of patches per side.
misconceptions.why_wrong: L78 glosses it as '14x14 patches': 14 is the patch size in pixels, so the number per side is 336/14 = 24, and 24^2 = 576 tokens.

predict.q: CLIP ViT-L/14@336px is given a 4000x3000 photo. How many patch tokens does the vision Transformer process?
predict.why: The photo is resized so the shorter side is 336 and center-cropped to 336x336 (L71-L72); 14-pixel patches (L78) give 24 x 24 = 576 tokens whatever the input size.
predict.targets_misconception: A ViT sees the image at whatever resolution it was captured; higher-resolution photos give it more tokens.
predict.distractor_from: 61,000: 'higher-resolution photos give it more tokens'; 196: '/14 is the number of patches per side'

transfer.q: A newer encoder keeps the 336x336 crop but is called ViT-H/8. Without computing the exact figure first, say whether the number of patch tokens per image goes up or down relative to ViT-L/14 and why; then give the count.
transfer.answer: Up: a smaller patch (8 pixels) cuts the same 336x336 crop into more pieces; (336/8)^2 = 42^2 = 1764 tokens, about 3x the 576 of ViT-L/14.
transfer.why: The patch size in pixels is the denominator (L78); tokens scale with (side/patch)^2, so halving the patch size nearly quadruples the tokens while the model-size letter (L vs H) does not enter.
transfer.varies: patch size (14 -> 8) with the model-size letter changed as a misleading surface cue

check.q: An encoder ViT-B/16@224px uses CLIP's preprocessing: resize so the shorter side is 224 pixels, then center-crop to 224x224. It is given a 1920x1080 photo. How many patch tokens does the vision Transformer process?
check.why: The resize and center crop force every image to 224x224 whatever its original size; '/16' is the patch side in pixels, so the crop is cut into 224/16 = 14 patches per side, 14^2 = 196 tokens.
check.varies: a different crop size (224) and patch size (16), with a non-square photo
check.invariant: tokens = (crop side / patch side)^2, fixed by preprocessing rather than the photo's resolution
check.targets_misconception: A ViT sees the image at whatever resolution it was captured; higher-resolution photos give it more tokens.

In 'ViT-L/14@336px', what do L, 14 and 336 each denote?

retrieval.q: Which activation does CLIP's text encoder return as the text embedding?

knowledge_points.label: Why caption pairs: augmentation-only self-supervision cannot group different images of the same kind
knowledge_points.statement: Augmentation-based self-supervision (SimCLR-style) trains an encoder to give the same embedding to transformed views of one image (crops, rotations, perturbations), which teaches invariances useful for low-level detail but never tells the model that two different images show the same kind of thing (one dog breed and another); pairing images with text supplies that higher-level semantic signal, which is why CLIP trains on (image, caption) pairs rather than on images alone.

anchors.quote: So the question I think is why they train on image-text pairs as opposed to images. ... So there is a line of work that tries to encode images into representations based on data augmentation.

I think this idea called SimCLR. ... They should have similar embeddings. ... And that's useful for low level details. ... But the problem is that you won't data augment your way from one type of dog to another dog. ... So by using the text, it gives you a higher level semantic representations

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (Q&A, 11:06-12:23). Its positives are exactly 'the same photo under crops, resizes and perturbations', which is the invariance the task needs, while negatives keep different photos apart. Caption supervision would pull together different photos with similar captions (two beach sunsets), which is the semantic grouping CLIP wants and this task must avoid.
transfer.why: The professor's contrast cuts both ways: augmentation learning is 'useful for low level details', text gives higher-level semantics (12:01-12:14). Which signal is right depends on whether the task's notion of 'same' is instance-level or category-level.

knowledge_points.label: CLIP embeddings carry caption-level semantics, not fine-grained detail
knowledge_points.statement: Trained on 400M web (image, text) pairs collected from 500K search queries, CLIP's image encoder learns whatever semantics noisy captions describe, which is enough for zero-shot ImageNet to beat a ResNet-50 trained on 1.2M labelled images, but its design choices were tuned for classification, so the representation is coarse and the 336 crop discards detail that tasks like OCR need.

anchors.quote: On ImageNet, zero-shot CLIP outperformed ResNet-50 trained on 1.2M ImageNet images
Encoding of images captures semantics given by (noisy) text ... Design decisions chosen based on image classification (not very fine-grained)
Searched for 500K queries, get ~20K (image, text) pairs per query ... Trained on 400M image-text pairs ... Didn't release the dataset
Reproduced in OpenCLIP (using LAION-5B dataset, which used CLIP for filtering)
Preserving high resolution is important (e.g., for OCR) ... CLIP resizes and crops to 336x336, which loses information

anchors.ref: CLIP paper §2.2 (data collection: up to 20,000 pairs per query, 400M total)
OpenCLIP reproduction on LAION (linked at L67)

anchors.quote: There are not too many details in the paper about the data. ... Roughly, you take a bunch of queries from somewhere and then you go search online for these and you mine a bunch of image and text pairs. ... And this resulted in 400 million image-text pairs.

So there was a data set called LAION-5B, which was released 5 billion images with textual descriptions. ... Interestingly, they actually used CLIP for the data filtering and then train OpenCLIP. ... So there's some bootstrapping happening.
on the ImageNet benchmark, 0 shot CLIP outperform a ResNet that was trained on 1.2 million ImageNet images. ... this was many, many hours of Amazon Mechanical Turk worker time to do this annotation.
And the zero shot technique is basically to explain I don't have slide support here. ... And then you basically take the dot product with the various labels and see which one's the highest.

But also another point is that these images are basically scraped from images on the web with textual text next to them or in the alt image. ... Because if you have an image and it's a dog, you don't need to say a dog. ... I mean, there was a lot of data filtering that is needed.

So we've encoded images using CLIP. ... And it captures the semantics of the image because it's paired with text. ... It is important to note that the design decisions here are based on image classification. ... So it's not very fine-grained.

And there's no one universal encoder let's say. ... For example, when we looked at CLIP, you only cared for classification to capture high level semantics. ... Whereas if you wanted to do OCR or whether you wanted to generate an image, then you need really fine-grained detail.

provenance.filtering_note: 500K queries x ~20K pairs each would be about 10B pairs, far more than the 400M stated at L65; the paper's wording is that results were approximately class-balanced by including up to 20,000 pairs per query, so '~20K' at L64 is a cap, not an average. That reconciliation is this thread's reading of the cited paper. The zero-shot headline (L85) is quoted without the accuracy number, which lives only in the paper. 'Noisy' (L93) refers to web alt-text. The LAION-5B remark (L67) carries a circularity the lecture does not dwell on: the reproduction's data was filtered by the model being reproduced. The OCR consequence (L159-L160) is said later, in the OneVision section, and is pulled here because it is the operational meaning of 'not very fine-grained'. Correction, partial (9:19-9:24): the note says LAION-5B's circularity is something 'the lecture does not dwell on'. He remarks on it, briefly: 'they actually used CLIP for the data filtering and then train OpenCLIP. So there's some bootstrapping happening.' Spoken evidence: the paper gives 'not too many details' about its data (8:26); zero-shot classification is described: take the dot product of the image with each label's text and pick the highest (18:04-18:28); captions are noisy because alt text rarely states the obvious, 'if you have an image and it's a dog, you don't need to say a dog' (19:38-19:52), so 'a lot of data filtering' was needed (20:03); the semantics come from the text because 'generally, text talks about the semantics' (21:40); the headline's weight is the annotation cost it avoids (17:36). The summary restates the KP as an asymmetry: there is 'no one universal encoder'; CLIP's high-level vectors suffice for classification, while OCR and generation need fine detail (1:15:39-1:16:09). The ImageNet accuracy is not read aloud.

prerequisites.note: What the embedding captures follows from what the ranking objective rewards (caption-level matching).
The 336 crop (L71-L72) is the concrete reason detail is lost (L160).

knowledge_points.label: SigLIP: a per-pair sigmoid loss decouples the objective from the batch size
knowledge_points.statement: SigLIP replaces CLIP's softmax over the batch (multiclass: which of the N candidates is the match) with an independent binary classification per (text, image) pair (aligned or not), so the loss no longer depends on normalising over the whole batch; this beats CLIP below 16K batch, saturates around 32K even though 1M is possible, and trained in 5 days on 32 TPUv4 versus CLIP's 10 days on 256 TPUv3.

anchors.quote: CLIP: multiclass classification for (text, image) versus (text, image') for all image' ... SigLIP: binary classification for (text, image) - aligned or not?
Decouple batch size from loss ... Better than CLIP for <16K batch sizes ... Go up to 1M batch size, but 32K is enough
CLIP: 10 days on 256 TPUv3 ... SigLIP: 5 days on 32 TPUv4 (lower FLOP/s than TPUv3) - much faster!
WebLI dataset: O(billion) (image, text) pairs ... Scraped from the Internet ... Used automatic OCR to extract text from images ... Keep 10% highest quality ... Supports 100 languages

anchors.ref: SigLIP paper, Algorithm 1 (sigmoid loss pseudocode, shown at L104) and Figure 1 (chunked device-parallel loss, shown at L116)
PaLI paper, WebLI dataset (linked at L107)

anchors.quote: And here, the main difference is that CLIP does multi-class classification. ... SigLIP, in some sense, is a lot simpler. ... It basically says for any given image text pair, are they aligned or not?
You take the embeddings. ... But now you're forming the labels which are minus 1 on the off-diagonal, and diagonals you have one. ... And then you do log_sigmoid.
At least in the initial paper, they were just operating on literally the same type of matrix. ... But at least in the initial version, this was fairly straightforward.

The main point of this paper was that it was much more efficient to train than CLIP. ... So CLIP was trained 10 days on 256 TPUv3, and CLIP was five days on 32v4s. ... In terms of flops per second, they're actually not. ... Actually, 60% slower or something.

So you have-- basically, if you recall your systems lecture, so this is you can think about it as DDP if you like ... So in the first pass, each device just computes all the losses on whatever image text pairs it has locally.
And then you send the text. ... So basically, device 1 gets T5 through T8. ... So you rotate around until you cover all the off-diagonal block entries.

If you change the batch size, it's a different loss function. ... Whereas for smaller batch size for CLIP, you have more variance but it's the same in expectation. ... And 32K was essentially their critical batch size.

provenance.filtering_note: The sigmoid loss itself is only in siglip-code.png (L104): -sum over all pairs of log sigmoid(z_ij * (t * x_i . y_j + b)) with z_ij = +1 on the diagonal and -1 elsewhere; the learnable bias and temperature are not mentioned in text. The parenthetical 'lower FLOP/s than TPUv3' (L115) only makes sense as the aggregate of 32 chips against 256, not per chip; that reading is this thread's. The device-parallel trick (each device computes its chunk of the pairwise loss and chunks are swapped, siglip-parallelism.png, L116) is the engineering reason the sigmoid form scales; the figure is recorded as shown. 'Better than CLIP for <16K' and '32K is enough' (L120-L121) are the paper's findings as read by the professor; the batch-size curves are not restated. WebLI's OCR text (L109) is a second source of captions, distinct from alt-text. Spoken evidence: the labels are +1 on the diagonal and -1 off it, then log-sigmoid (23:44-23:53, reading siglip-code.png; the learnable temperature and bias are not mentioned aloud); the original paper used no special negative sampling, 'literally the same type of matrix' (Q&A 24:03-24:46); the chunked device-parallel loss (siglip-parallelism.png) is narrated: like DDP each device holds some pairs, first computes the losses on its local pairs, then text chunks rotate between devices 'until you cover all the off-diagonal block entries' (26:24-27:38); part of the speedup may be engineering, since 'CLIP probably did not try to optimize the code for the maximum throughput' (26:09); 'If you change the batch size, it's a different loss function' for CLIP (27:51); 32K is 'essentially their critical batch size' (28:30), linking to the batch-size lectures. On L115's '(lower FLOP/s than TPUv3)': aloud, 'you might think, oh, v4s actually should be faster than v3. In terms of flops per second, they're actually not ... But at this scale, it's really actually not faster. Actually, 60% slower or something' (25:46-26:04). Read per chip this is wrong (TPUv4 peaks around 275 bf16 TFLOP/s against about 123 for TPUv3; this thread's knowledge, not the lecture's); read as 32 chips against 256 ('at this scale') it supports this thread's aggregate reading, since 32 × 275 against 256 × 123 is about 72% less. Spoken slips (not imported): 'CLIP was five days on 32v4s' (25:36) means SigLIP; 'for smaller batch size for CLIP, you have more variance but it's the same in expectation' (28:10) also means SigLIP. 'The same in expectation' is itself loose: a larger batch gives each image more negatives, which is why the second misconception's why_wrong keeps a batch dependence (this thread's note). 'the diagonal are negative examples' (23:23) is a slip or caption error for 'off-diagonal', put right in the code walk at 23:44.

knowledge_points.label: Standard VLM template: vision encoder + projector + language model
knowledge_points.statement: Every VLM in the lecture is a pretrained vision encoder (CLIP or SigLIP) producing a grid of continuous patch features, a projector that maps those features into the language model's embedding space (LLaVA: one linear layer W; OneVision: a 2-layer MLP; Qwen-VL: one cross-attention layer with 2D positional encodings that compresses to a fixed 256 tokens), and a pretrained decoder LM (Vicuna, Qwen-2 72B, Qwen-3) that reads the projected image tokens inline with text tokens.

anchors.quote: Standard VLM template: vision encoder + projector + LM
Encode images with CLIP (ViT-L/14) ... Linear projection (W) into embedding space (Flamingo and Q-former are more complex)
Vision encoder: CLIP ... Text decoder: Vicuna (LLaMA fine-tuned on ShareGPT conversations)
Vision encoder: SigLIP (use grid features before and after last Transformer layer) ... Text decoder: Qwen-2 72B ... Projector: 2-layer MLP
Vision encoder: OpenCLIP's ViT-bigC (14x14 patches) ... Adaptor: one layer cross-attention, incorporate 2D positional encodings, maps to fixed length of 256 ... Special tokens: , ,
DeepStack: cross-layer fusion to inject visual information into multiple layers
So far: VLMs encode images (via CLIP or SigLIP), inject into LM

anchors.ref: LLaVA architecture figure (llava-architecture.png, shown at L140)

anchors.quote: These are image encoders that take an image, in this version, just a fixed size image, 336 by 336, let's say, and maps it into a vector, OK, which contains some semantics.

And I'm going to talk about two families of models, LLaVA and Qwen. ... So this is going to be more of a flavor of mid-training or post-training, where we take an existing image encoder. ... We take an existing LLM, and then we're going to stitch it together

But this vector isn't really in the same space, so to speak, as the text. ... So then they multiply by a matrix W to get another vector, which is in the same space as the text embeddings. ... OK, so we're in some sense converting these images into textual tokens.
They upgrade it to SigLIP. ... is a two-layer MLP instead of a linear projection. ... OK, so it's like you have a system and you're just upgrading the parts.

And for the adapter, they did one layer of cross-attention, incorporate 2D positional embeddings and maps to a fixed size of 256, which is a little bit-- I guess this will be changed later because this is definitely not very dynamic, but neither is the vision encoder at this point.

So remember we started the adapter is the thing that connects the vision encoder to the language model. ... And we're basically going to basically add these directly into the residual stream of the language model.

OK, the reason is that the vision encoder is in some sense doing a very local operation. ... So most of the capabilities of the model are still in the language model. ... And the VIT is generally less than a billion, parameters.

provenance.filtering_note: The template is named only in the OneVision summary (L190) but every section instantiates it, so it is pulled forward. OneVision's 'grid features before and after last Transformer layer' (L154) says the projector gets the per-patch grid, not CLIP's pooled embedding; the lecture does not say how the two grids are combined. Qwen-VL's 'ViT-bigC' (L199) is the file's spelling of OpenCLIP's ViT-bigG. transfer.q: Two VLMs take a 1344x1344 document scan. Model A uses LLaVA's per-patch linear projector on a tiled encoder output; Model B uses Qwen-VL's one-layer cross-attention adaptor. Predict which model's language-model sequence length depends on the scan's resolution and which does not, and name the mechanism in each case.
transfer.answer: Model A: sequence length grows with resolution because a per-patch linear map emits one LM token per encoder patch; Model B: fixed, because the cross-attention adaptor uses a fixed set of learned queries and 'maps to fixed length of 256' whatever the number of patches.
transfer.why: L139 (linear projection per patch) versus L200 (cross-attention adaptor to fixed length 256). A per-patch map preserves count; a query-based adaptor fixes it.
transfer.varies: projector type (per-patch linear vs cross-attention with fixed queries), functional dimension
transfer.invariant: the encoder emits one feature per patch; only the projector decides how many LM tokens result

check.q: A VLM applies a LLaVA-style single linear projector to every patch feature of a ViT with 14-pixel patches run on a 448x448 input (no tiling, no pooling). How many image tokens enter the language model?

knowledge_points.label: Visual instruction data is synthesised from text annotations by a text-only LLM
knowledge_points.statement: LLaVA built its 158K visual-instruction examples by prompting GPT-4 with MS COCO's human captions and bounding-box object lists (never the pixels) to write questions and conversations, then pairing those with the original images; later work (LLaVA-OneVision) keeps the pattern, with most effort going into curating synthesised, task-specific data under a quality-over-quantity philosophy.

anchors.quote: MS COCO has images annotated with bounding boxes and Mechanical Turk captions ... Prompt GPT-4 with captions or detected objects and generate questions or conversations ... Pair generations with original images ... 158K examples
Philosophy: quality over quantity
Most work goes into data curation (heavy on synthesized, task-specific data) ... Open-source (released model weights and data)
Lots of data work, but not many details

anchors.ref: LLaVA data-generation figure (llava-gen.png, shown at L135) and example (llava-example.png, L145)
OneVision data composition figures (llava-onevision-data-1/2.png, shown at L174-L175)

anchors.quote: So the data that they used was based on MS COCO. ... So they basically synthesized a data set for their model. ... So they prompted GPT-4 with the captions or the detected objects and GPT-4 to generate questions or conversations.

And then you ask GPT-4, generate me a conversation and you might get a question and an answer. ... You might ask GPT-4 generate me a detailed description. ... And then you can ask GPT-4 to generate complex reasoning. ... OK, so those are synthesized data, 158,000 examples.

Another way to interpret this is that it's very targeted data. ... So this is definitely post-training territory ... And this work is also unabashedly, basically, distilling GPT-4 models so that they can get the best performance ... But this is what you do if you don't have an annotation budget.

There's a lot of work that goes into the data curation. ... They lean pretty heavily into synthesize task-specific data. ... The nice thing about the LLaVA series is that it's one of the few works that open sources. ... They're not just the model weights, but also the data.
There's a lot of data work that happens. ... Not too many details about the data and the data mix in these later Qwen models.

transfer.invariant: the generator sees only the textual annotation, so groundedness is bounded by what that annotation encodes

knowledge_points.label: VLM training is staged: train the connector first, unfreeze progressively, instruction-tune last
knowledge_points.statement: VLMs are trained in stages that differ in which parameters receive gradients and on what data: LLaVA trains only the projector W with both encoder and LM frozen (alignment) and then W plus the LM (fine-tuning); Qwen-VL trains encoder plus adaptor on large low-quality data with the LM frozen, then everything at higher resolution on higher-quality data, then adaptor plus LM on instruction data with the encoder frozen; Qwen2-VL and Qwen3-VL follow the same shape, Qwen3-VL ending with SFT on long chain-of-thought data, distillation and RL.

anchors.quote: Stage 1 (alignment): freeze vision encoder and language model, only train W ... Stage 2 (fine-tuning): freeze vision encoder and train W and language model

Stage 1: large-scale low quality data; freeze LM, train vision encoder + adaptor ... Stage 2: higher quality task-specific data, increase resolution; train all parameters ... Stage 3: instruction tuning data; freeze visual encoder, train adaptor + LM

Initialize LM with Qwen2 and vision encoder from DFN ... Training (similar to Qwen-VL): ... Stage 1: train only visual encoder ... Stage 2: train all parameters ... Stage 3: train language model on instruction following datasets
Pre-training has 4 stages (train adapter, train all parameters on 8K, 32K, 256K lengths) ... Post-training: SFT on long CoT data, knowledge distillation, RL
Philosophy: easier to harder
Stage 1 (80%): large-scale, unsupervised (2.9T text tokens, 1.5T text/image tokens, 400B text/image interleaved tokens) ... Stage 2 (20%): 50% of stage 1 data, 50% of high quality data

anchors.ref: Qwen-VL three-stage figure and per-stage data tables (qwen-vl-stages.png, qwen-vl-stage1/2.png, shown at L204-L208)
Qwen3-VL pre-training stage table (qwen3-vl-pretraining.png, shown at L256)

anchors.quote: So to train this model, they do it in two stages. ... The first stage is that they freeze the vision encoder and the language model and only train this matrix W. ... So the goal of training W is that they look like natural language token embeddings.
And the second stage is that they now still freeze a vision encoder and then train W and the language model. ... So they're fine-tuning the language model on their data.

I'm not sure there's any particular principled reason for this, except for this second stage is trying to put high quality data but more focused on knowledge. ... And the final stage is focusing on examples that look like your downstream tasks.

I mean, they call it pre-training but you're not pre-training from scratch. ... They freeze the language model and train the vision encoder and adapter. ... So this is a bit different from the LLaVA models, in that, they train the vision encoder at this point.
And finally, stage 3 is instruction tuning data. ... You freeze the visual encoder and you train the adapter and the language model.

Pre-training has actually four stages. ... So they first train the adapter. ... This is the same as all of these models. ... from 8K, to 32K, to 256K. ... And then for post-training, they do SFT on long chain of thought data, knowledge distillation, and then some reinforcement learning.

And it definitely has to be pre-trained because otherwise it doesn't make sense to align it. ... And you're just training the adapter to connect the given vision encoder with a given language model. ... There's not an adaptive threshold here.

provenance.filtering_note: Which parameters are frozen is stated for LLaVA and Qwen-VL; for Qwen2-VL the lecture says 'train only visual encoder' in stage 1 (L228) without saying whether the merger/adaptor is included, and for Qwen3-VL only 'train adapter' then 'train all parameters' (L255). The dataset sizes and mixture ratios per stage live in figures (L204-L208, L256) and are not restated, except Chameleon's text-stated token counts (L288-L289), which are the professor's reading of the paper. 'Easier to harder' (L178) refers to OneVision's curriculum table (L179, shown). Why one would freeze the LM while training the encoder on low-quality data (to protect the LM) is this thread's gloss; the lecture states the schedule, not the reason. The post-training line (L257) is the file's only alignment content. Spoken evidence: the reason for an alignment stage is given for LLaVA: with a random W the projected images 'are not embeddings, representing any natural language token', so stage 1 trains W alone until they 'look like natural language token embeddings' (33:39-34:09); the LM must already be pre-trained, or 'it doesn't make sense to align it', and stage 1 runs for a fixed token budget with 'not an adaptive threshold' (Q&A 1:03:31-1:03:56; the '67 billion tokens' he reads off a figure is not restated). OneVision's three stages: 'I'm not sure there's any particular principled reason for this', stage 2 is high-quality knowledge data and stage 3 data that looks like the downstream tasks (43:04-43:30). Qwen-VL's stage 1 is called pre-training but is 'not pre-training from scratch', and unlike LLaVA it trains the encoder (47:19-47:51); its stage-1 data is read as '1.4 billion examples' (47:51, a figure reading, not restated). Qwen3-VL: training the adapter first is 'the same as all of these models', then 8K, 32K and 256K stages, with 'most of the tokens ... in the stages 2 and 3' (58:11-58:25, figure reading). Why Qwen-VL freezes the LM while training the encoder on low-quality data is still not said aloud; that gloss stays this thread's.

The last stage in every recipe consumes instruction data (L144, L209, L230).

'SFT on long CoT data, knowledge distillation, RL' (L257) is the R1-style ordering lecture 16 described.
Chameleon's stage 2 (20% of training, half high-quality data, L289) is the same mix-high-quality-data-into-the-end-of-pretraining move.

transfer.q: A team has a strong instruction-tuned LM, a weak vision encoder trained on little data, and 2B noisy web image-caption pairs plus 50K hand-checked Q/A pairs.
