knowledge_points.label: AnyRes: tile high-resolution images into encoder-sized pieces under a shared token budget
knowledge_points.statement: Because resizing and cropping to 336x336 destroys detail (OCR), AnyRes splits a high-resolution image into an a x b grid of pieces each at the encoder's native resolution, encodes every piece and concatenates the tokens (a x b times as many), bilinearly downsampling when the total would exceed the token budget; LLaVA-OneVision then spends roughly the same total token length on each input type: one image at high resolution, several images at base resolution each, or many video frames at low resolution each.

anchors.quote: Preserving high resolution is important (e.g., for OCR) ... CLIP resizes and crops to 336x336, which loses information ... Solution: AnyRes, introduced in LLaVA 1.5 ... Break up image into a x b pieces (matching resolution of vision encoder), encode, concatenate ... If too many tokens (original image is too high resolution), then use bilinear interpolation

Handle 3 types of input (single image, multiple images, video): ... Goal: make all of the modalities produce roughly the same length ... Single image: use higher resolution ... Multiple images: use base resolution for each image ... Video: use lower resolution for each frame
Handle multiple images, video

anchors.ref: LLaVA-1.5 high-resolution grid scheme (linked at L161)
OneVision AnyRes and per-modality token allocation figures (llava-onevision-anyres.png L164, llava-onevision-modalities.png L167)

anchors.quote: So one thing that they wanted to do is to do OCR. ... Otherwise, a J looks like an I, and that's not good. ... And clearly, if you have a document and you crop to 336 by 336, you can't read it.

You break up an image into multiple pieces. ... And then you concatenate the vectors. ... So rather than downsampling, you're just going to crop and look at different parts of image. ... And now if you have really super high resolution images or videos then, you get too many tokens.
But the idea behind AnyRes is that it's adaptive. ... And this is nice because the transformer is already adaptive. ... So it turns out images can be any resolution.
They do downsample and have one path, which is basically a downsampled encoding of the entire paper. ... And if you have too many, then you reduce that the number of patches by interpolation.

but they put their thumb on the scale a little bit because they want to make sure all the modalities are roughly comparable. ... Because videos can be very long, they don't want their data set to be dominated by a bunch of repetitive frames.

So for a single image, they basically have the full image downsampled and then a bunch of crops up to N crops there, up to 9. ... If I have multiple images, I'm just going to look at it from afar. ... they only use up to 32 frames

provenance.filtering_note: The lecture gives no numbers for AnyRes; with a 336-pixel encoder and 14-pixel patches each piece is 576 tokens and an a x b grid is a*b*576 (this thread's arithmetic from L78 and L162). The lecture omits that LLaVA-1.5's grid scheme also appends a downscaled whole-image thumbnail, and that OneVision's figure fixes concrete per-modality token counts; those numbers are in the figures (L164, L167) and the papers and are not restated. 'Bilinear interpolation' (L163) is applied to the encoded feature grid to shrink the token count, not to the pixels; the lecture does not say which. The attribution 'introduced in LLaVA 1.5' with a link to the Improved Baselines PDF is kept as said; the name AnyRes is usually associated with LLaVA-NeXT (listed at L150). Correction (39:07-39:26): the note says the lecture omits that the grid scheme also appends a downscaled whole-image view. Reading the OneVision figure aloud: 'They do downsample and have one path, which is basically a downsampled encoding of the entire paper', then the encoder-sized chunks. Correction, partial (40:09-40:37): the note says the per-modality numbers live only in the figures; aloud he reads 'up to 9' crops for a single image and 'up to 32 frames' for video (figure readings, not restated as this thread's numbers). Spoken evidence: why resolution matters for OCR, 'a J looks like an I' (37:20); AnyRes 'is adaptive', which suits a Transformer that already handles any sequence length (38:35-38:51); the interpolation reduces 'the number of patches' (39:26), which supports this thread's reading that it acts on the feature grid; why the per-modality budget: 'videos can be very long, they don't want their data set to be dominated by a bunch of repetitive frames' (39:43-40:07), so a single image is looked at 'more carefully' and multiple images 'from afar' (40:28-40:31). L161's attribution to LLaVA 1.5 is repeated (37:36).

prerequisites.note: The 336 crop and 576-token patch count are what tiling multiplies.
The OCR failure (L159-L160) is the motivation.
Tiles are encoded and concatenated before the projector (L162).

external_prerequisites.note: Tiles trade detail for sequence length the way a smaller vocabulary trades compression for length.

misconceptions.belief: Feeding a higher-resolution image to a VLM improves detail at no cost in sequence length.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each extra 336x336 piece adds another full set of 576 tokens (L162); a 2x2 grid is 4x the tokens, and beyond the budget the model has to interpolate tokens away (L163).

misconceptions.belief: Video is handled by giving every frame the same resolution a single image gets.
misconceptions.why_wrong: OneVision's goal is that all input types 'produce roughly the same length' (L166), so video frames get lower resolution each (L170) and multiple images get base resolution (L169); only a single image gets the high-resolution tiling (L168).

predict.q: With a 336-pixel encoder (576 tokens per piece) and no budget cap, a 1344x1344 image is tiled by AnyRes. How many visual tokens reach the LM, compared with the 576 of a plain CLIP crop?
choices: 2304 (4x, since the side doubled twice)
576 (tiling changes detail, not count)
predict.why: 1344/336 = 4 pieces per side, so a = b = 4 and 16 x 576 = 9216 (L162, with the 576 from L78). Tokens scale with area, not side length.
predict.targets_misconception: Feeding a higher-resolution image to a VLM improves detail at no cost in sequence length.
predict.distractor_from: 2304: scaling tokens with side length rather than area; 576: 'higher resolution at no cost in sequence length'

transfer.q: OneVision wants a 32-frame video clip to cost roughly the same tokens as one 2x2-tiled single image (2304 tokens). Without computing first, say whether each frame gets more or fewer tokens than a plain 336 crop (576) and what the model does to achieve it; then give the per-frame number.
transfer.answer: Fewer: each frame must be encoded at a lower effective resolution, with its token grid interpolated down to fit; 2304 / 32 = 72 tokens per frame, an 8x reduction from 576.
transfer.why: L166 (same length across input types), L170 (lower resolution per frame), L163 (bilinear interpolation when there are too many tokens).
transfer.varies: input type (video of 32 frames instead of a single image), modality dimension
transfer.invariant: a shared total token budget across input types

check.q: OneVision-style budgeting: a single image tiled 3x3 at 576 tokens per piece sets the budget (9 x 576 = 5,184 tokens). A 64-frame video must cost the same total. How many tokens does each frame get?
check.why: Total budget 5,184 / 64 frames = 81 tokens per frame, a 7x reduction from 576. Each frame's grid is downsampled (bilinear interpolation) to fit, the 'many frames at low resolution' case of L165-L170.
check.varies: a 3x3-tiled budget and 64 frames, instead of 2x2 and 32
check.invariant: all input types share roughly the same total token length, so per-frame tokens = budget / frames
check.targets_misconception: Video is handled by giving every frame the same resolution a single image gets.

retrieval.q: What task does the lecture give as the reason high resolution must be preserved?
retrieval.answer: OCR.

retrieval.q: Describe the three steps of AnyRes.
retrieval.answer: Break the image into a x b pieces matching the encoder's resolution, encode each, concatenate.

retrieval.q: What does OneVision do when a tiled image would produce too many tokens?
retrieval.answer: Bilinear interpolation to reduce the token count.

retrieval.q: How does OneVision allocate resolution across single image, multiple images and video?
retrieval.answer: Single image: higher resolution; multiple images: base resolution each; video: lower resolution per frame.

prompts.self_explain: Why would a designer want video, multi-image and single-image inputs to produce roughly the same token length rather than letting each take what it needs?

presentations.notice: In AnyRes mode the count jumps by a whole tile of 576 each time width or height passes a multiple of 336, so it grows with area (4 × 4 tiles give 16×, not 4×). Pick a budget equal to one tiled image and add video seconds: the same total is split across the frames, and each frame gets far fewer tokens than one 576-token crop.
listen for: the downsampled whole view plus encoder-sized crops, then why single images, multiple images and video get different resolutions

knowledge_points.label: Capabilities trained on single images transfer to multi-image, video and GUI tasks
knowledge_points.statement: When all input types share one token interface and budget, skills learned from single-image data generalise: diagram and chart understanding carries to multi-image inputs, OCR from single images plus relational reasoning from multi-image data combine into GUI-agent behaviour, and visual prompting (a drawn circle) learned on single images works on video frames.

anchors.quote: Transfer between modalities: ... Single image data for diagrams and charts, but generalize to multi-image
OCR on single image data, relational reasoning from multi-image data, generalize to GUI-based agents
Visual prompting (circle) in single images, generalize to videos
Goal: make all of the modalities produce roughly the same length

anchors.ref: OneVision transfer examples S1, S2, S8 (llava-onevision-transfer-s1/s2/s8.png, shown at L183, L185, L187)

anchors.quote: OK, so one thing that they found in this paper, which was interesting, is that you get transfer between modalities. ... So at training time, you never saw an example where you have a table and a chart and you're asking questions about it.

At training time, you only have OCR data on single image data, and you only have relational reasoning from multiple images. ... But you can generalize to these cases which are useful for powering GUI agents
And this type of data only exists for single images. ... And now it can generalize to videos where the user says describe the player highlighted in the video.
You're basically targeting each of these tasks. ... But if you have enough tasks, these models seem to do some transfer, which is, I guess, reassuring.

provenance.filtering_note: The evidence is three qualitative example figures from the OneVision paper (L183, L185, L187), each one case; no benchmark numbers are given and none are restated. The link from the shared token interface (L166) to transfer is the lecture's implicit argument (the transfer bullets follow the modality-length design in the same section), made explicit here as this thread's reading. 'Generalize' in the bullets means zero-shot on the target input type without task-specific training data, which the lecture does not spell out. Correction (43:49-44:05): the note says the lecture does not spell out that 'generalize' means zero-shot on the new input type. Aloud: 'at training time, you never saw an example where you have a table and a chart ... But at test time, you have two images'. Spoken evidence: his reading of the result: it looks like per-task supervised learning, 'But if you have enough tasks, these models seem to do some transfer, which is, I guess, reassuring' (45:06-45:27). The shared token interface is still not named aloud as the cause; that link stays this thread's reading.

prerequisites.note: The shared-length design (L166-L170) precedes the transfer claims (L181-L187) in the same section.
The transferred skills are those the task-specific synthesised data taught (L191).

misconceptions.belief: A VLM can only do a task on the input type (single image, multi-image, video) it was trained on for that task.
misconceptions.why_wrong: All three examples (L182, L184, L186) are skills trained on one input type and exercised on another; the lecture presents this as a design payoff of the unified interface.

misconceptions.belief: Transfer to a new task (GUI agents) requires GUI training data.
misconceptions.why_wrong: L184 describes GUI-agent behaviour arising from OCR learned on single images combined with relational reasoning learned on multi-image data, with no GUI data named.

predict.q: A OneVision-style model was trained to answer questions about single bar charts and never saw two charts in one prompt. It is given two charts and asked which has the higher 2023 bar. According to the lecture, what should you expect?
choices: it generalises: single-image chart skill transfers to the multi-image input
it fails until multi-image chart data is added
it answers about only the first chart because multi-image inputs are truncated
predict.answer: it generalises: single-image chart skill transfers to the multi-image input
predict.why: L182: 'Single image data for diagrams and charts, but generalize to multi-image'; multiple images are encoded at base resolution under the same token budget (L169), not truncated.
predict.targets_misconception: A VLM can only do a task on the input type (single image, multi-image, video) it was trained on for that task.
predict.distractor_from: fails until data added: 'only the trained input type'; truncated: misreading the shared-length budget (L166) as dropping images

transfer.q: A team has strong single-image OCR data and a multi-image dataset of 'which object moved between these two photos' questions, and no screen recordings. Predict whether the lecture's evidence supports expecting the model to operate a desktop GUI from screenshots, and name the two ingredient skills.
transfer.answer: Yes, the lecture's example supports it: OCR from single images (read the labels and menus) combined with relational reasoning from multi-image data (what changed between screens) is exactly the combination it says generalises to GUI-based agents without GUI data.
transfer.why: L184: 'OCR on single image data, relational reasoning from multi-image data, generalize to GUI-based agents'.
transfer.varies: the target task (desktop GUI) and the specific source datasets, functional dimension
transfer.invariant: the composed skill is available only if both ingredient skills exist and share the same token interface

check.q: A OneVision-style model learned to answer questions about a region circled in red on single images, and never saw a circle drawn on a video. It is given a video whose first frame has a circled object and asked what that object does. Per the lecture, what should you expect?
choices: it works only after some video-specific circle data
it fails: it never saw circles drawn on video frames
it generalises: circle prompting transfers to video
check.answer: it generalises: circle prompting transfers to video
check.why: L186: visual prompting (a circle) learned on single images generalises to videos, because all input types share one token interface and budget (L166).
check.varies: the transferred skill is visual prompting to video rather than OCR plus relations to GUIs
check.invariant: with a shared token interface, single-image skills transfer to other input types
check.targets_misconception: A VLM can only do a task on the input type (single image, multi-image, video) it was trained on for that task.
distractor_from: 'it fails: it never saw circles drawn on video frames' <- misconception: 'A VLM can only do a task on the input type (single image, multi-image, video) it was trained on for that task.'
'it works only after some video-specific circle data' <- misconception: 'Transfer to a new task (GUI agents) requires GUI training data.'

retrieval.q: Which skill learned on single images does the lecture say transfers to video?
retrieval.answer: Visual prompting: following a mark such as a circle drawn on the image.

retrieval.q: Which two source skills does the lecture say combine into GUI-agent behaviour?
retrieval.answer: OCR learned on single images and relational reasoning learned on multi-image data.

retrieval.q: What design goal of LLaVA-OneVision's inputs makes transfer across single images, multiple images and video plausible?
retrieval.answer: All input types produce roughly the same token length through one interface.

prompts.self_explain: Why would giving video frames and single images the same token format make a skill learned on one usable on the other?

presentations.notice: listen for: transfer means a combination never seen in training (a table and a chart in two images) works at test time

knowledge_points.label: Qwen2-VL dynamic resolution: tokens = patches / 4 (+2), video capped at 16384 tokens
knowledge_points.statement: Qwen2-VL encodes each image at its native resolution with a 14-pixel-patch ViT (675M parameters) and merges every 2x2 block of patch features into one LM token, so a 224x224 image gives (224/14)^2 = 256 patches and 64 merged tokens, which the lecture reports as 66 (the two extra are the vision start/end delimiters per the paper); token count grows with pixel area, and video is sampled at 2 frames per second under a 16384-token cap.

anchors.quote: Visual encoder: larger ViT (675M) ... Key: dynamic resolution to handle varying resolutions ... Each 224 x 224 patch encoded with ViT/14, compress every 2x2 => 66 tokens ... Video: sample 2 frames/sec, max 16384 tokens
Initialize LM with Qwen2 and vision encoder from DFN

anchors.ref: Qwen2-VL §2.1 naive dynamic resolution (224x224 -> 66 tokens; <|vision_start|>/<|vision_end|> delimiters), architecture figure (qwen2-vl-architecture.png, shown at L218)

anchors.quote: So use a larger vision encoder. ... They also started doing dynamic resolution. ... So let's say you have this picture here, that might be mapped to 11,000 tokens. ... This tiny picture of an equation might be only mapped to 8 tokens and so on and so forth.

where each 224 by 224 patch is encoded with a VIT. ... And then trying to reduce the contact size, they compress every 2 by 2 into 1 so that they ultimately edge every patch generates 66 tokens. ... For eight videos, they sample 2 frames a second but max out at 16,000 tokens.

provenance.filtering_note: 256 patches and 64 merged tokens are this thread's arithmetic from L220; the lecture states 66 and does not say where the extra two come from. The Qwen2-VL paper wraps each image's tokens in <|vision_start|> and <|vision_end|>, which accounts for 66; that is this thread's reading of the cited paper, not lecture content. 'Each 224 x 224 patch' (L220) uses 'patch' for the image, not for the 14-pixel ViT patch. The 2x2 'compress' is an MLP merger in the paper; the lecture does not name it. The 16384 cap (L221) is for video; whether images share it is not stated. The capabilities figure (L233) and the 675M figure are recorded as said/shown. Spoken evidence: dynamic resolution is 'the main thing' in Qwen2-VL (49:32), needed for video (49:42); the architecture figure is read aloud: a large picture 'might be mapped to 11,000 tokens', a tiny equation 'only ... 8 tokens' (49:47-50:00; figure values, not restated as this thread's); '66 tokens' per 224x224 is repeated (50:36), with nothing on where the extra two come from; the video cap 'max out at 16,000 tokens' rounds L221's 16384. He calls it 'the same idea AnyRes idea from LLaVA' (50:13), though the code's mechanism is native resolution with patch merging, not tiling. Imprecision (50:26): 'the VIT that they started with is the OpenCLIP bit', which 'gets fine-tuned'; L226 says the encoder is initialized from DFN.

prerequisites.note: Same 14-pixel patch arithmetic, now without the fixed crop.
Dynamic resolution is the alternative to tiling: native resolution instead of a grid of fixed pieces, with the same budget problem.

external_prerequisites.note: The 2x2 merge is a compression step: fewer, coarser tokens per image, as a larger vocabulary gives fewer tokens per text.

misconceptions.belief: Doubling an image's side length doubles its token count.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Patches tile the area: 448x448 has (448/14)^2 = 1024 patches, four times 224x224's 256, and after the 2x2 merge 256 tokens versus 64 (L220). Tokens scale with pixel area.

misconceptions.belief: The 2x2 merge means the ViT runs on 28-pixel patches.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The ViT still processes 14-pixel patches (L220: 'ViT/14'); the merge compresses groups of four output features into one LM token afterwards, so the encoder cost is set by patches and the LM cost by tokens.

predict.q: Qwen2-VL is given a 448x448 image. Counting the same two extra tokens that make the 224x224 example 66, how many visual tokens does the LM receive?
predict.why: (448/14)^2 = 1024 patches; 2x2 merge gives 256; plus the same 2 delimiters that turn 64 into 66 at L220 gives 258. Doubling the side quadruples patches.
predict.targets_misconception: Doubling an image's side length doubles its token count.
predict.distractor_from: 132: 'doubling the side doubles tokens'; 66: treating dynamic resolution like CLIP's fixed crop (token count independent of input)

transfer.q: A 60-second clip is sampled at Qwen2-VL's 2 frames per second, each frame 448x448 (258 tokens at that size). First say whether it fits the 16384-token video cap and why; then say what per-frame token allowance the cap leaves and roughly what square frame size that corresponds to.
transfer.answer: No: 120 frames x 258 = 30,960 tokens, almost 2x the cap, because tokens grow with frames x area; the cap allows about 16384 / 120 = 136 tokens per frame, i.e. about 134 x 4 = 536 patches, roughly a 23 x 23 patch grid or about 320x320 pixels per frame.
transfer.why: L221 (2 frames/sec, max 16384 tokens) with the patch and 2x2-merge arithmetic of L220; the cap forces lower resolution per frame, the same trade OneVision made (L170).
transfer.varies: the multiplier is time (frames) rather than spatial tiles, and the cap binds
transfer.invariant: tokens per frame = patches / 4 + 2 with 14-pixel patches; the total must stay under 16384

check.q: Qwen2-VL encodes an image at native resolution with 14-pixel patches and merges every 2x2 block of patches into one LM token, then adds the same 2 delimiter tokens that make a 224x224 image cost 66. How many visual tokens does a 672x336 image cost?
check.why: 672/14 = 48 and 336/14 = 24 patches per side, 1,152 patches in all; the 2x2 merge gives 288 tokens; plus 2 delimiters = 290. Token count grows with pixel area, not side length.
check.varies: a non-square image with new dimensions instead of a video-cap budget
check.targets_misconception: Doubling an image's side length doubles its token count.

retrieval.q: In Qwen2-VL, what does a 224x224 image become?
retrieval.answer: Encoded with ViT/14, every 2x2 compressed, giving 66 tokens.

retrieval.q: How does Qwen2-VL sample video and what is the token cap?
retrieval.answer: 2 frames per second, at most 16384 tokens.

retrieval.q: What is the 'key' idea of Qwen2-VL's visual encoder?
retrieval.answer: Dynamic resolution: handling varying input resolutions natively.

retrieval.q: From where are Qwen2-VL's LM and vision encoder initialised?
retrieval.answer: LM from Qwen2; vision encoder from DFN.

prompts.self_explain: Why merge 2x2 patch features before the LM instead of using 28-pixel patches in the ViT from the start?

presentations.notice: In native mode tokens follow pixel area: 224 gives 66 and 448 gives 258, because doubling the side quadruples the patches. With 60 s of video at 2 frames/s and the 16384 budget, the readout goes over budget and prints the per-frame allowance and the square frame size that fits.
listen for: token count follows image size (11,000 tokens against 8), the 2x2 merge, and 2 fps video capped near 16K tokens

knowledge_points.label: MRoPE: rotary position across time, width and height, interleaved across frequency bands
knowledge_points.statement: Multimodal RoPE gives each visual token a position along three axes (temporal, width, height) instead of one, encoded in the rotary dimensions; Qwen3-VL interleaves the axes across the frequency bands ([t w h t w h ...] rather than [t t t t w w w w h h h h]) so that every axis gets both low- and high-frequency dimensions, and adds explicit video timestamps as separate tokens rather than relying on the position embedding to convey absolute time.

anchors.quote: Multimodal Rotary Position Embedding (MRoPE):

Interleaved MRoPE: distribute all axes (temporal, width, height) to low- and high-frequency bands ... [t w h t w h t w h t w h] rather than [t t t t w w w w h h h h] ... Add explicit video timestamps (as separate tokens rather in positional embeddings)
incorporate 2D positional encodings

anchors.ref: Qwen2-VL MRoPE figure (qwen2-vl-mrope.png, shown at L224)
Qwen3-VL interleaved MRoPE and timestamp tokens (L246-L248)

anchors.quote: So they used this idea called multimodal rotary, multimodal RoPE. ... And the idea behind RoPE is that you have embedding such that the inner product between the vectors depends only on the distance. ... So the distance is defined in 1D by just the number of tokens.

So each position, each patch now is a triple defined by the coordinates. ... for every dimension, you compute the RoPE and then you concatenate. ... Although, later, with Qwen-3, we'll see how this is actually a bit suboptimal.

And the problem, if you remember RoPE is that each component refers represents a different frequency. ... So they basically interleave them when they realize that. ... And they now all the axes are exposed to both low and high frequency.

But before, the time stamp was implicit in the positional encodings. ... But here, they made the time explicit. ... And they found this to be helpful presumably because it's something that you can directly refer to, like what happened after two seconds.

provenance.filtering_note: MRoPE's basic mechanism is given only as a figure (L224): the rotary dimensions are split into groups indexed by temporal, height and width position ids, with text tokens getting identical ids on all three axes; that description is this thread's reading of the Qwen2-VL figure and paper, not lecture text. The lecture's own text is the Qwen3-VL change (L246-L248). Which end of the rotary dimension vector is high-frequency is not stated; in standard RoPE (lecture 3) frequencies decrease along the dimension index, so a blocked layout gives one axis only fast-rotating dimensions and another only slow ones; this is the reason interleaving helps, and it is inference from lecture 3's RoPE, not stated here. 'Rather in positional embeddings' (L248) reads as 'rather than in'. Correction (51:47-52:04): the note says MRoPE's basic mechanism is given only as a figure and that the description is this thread's reading. Aloud: 'each patch now is a triple defined by the coordinates' (height, width, time), and 'for every dimension, you compute the RoPE and then you concatenate', i.e. the blocked layout. Text tokens sharing one id on all three axes is still only in the figure and paper. Correction (54:28-54:48): the note says the reason interleaving helps is inference from lecture 3's RoPE, 'not stated here'. It is stated: 'each component ... represents a different frequency. So this would mean that maybe all the temporal dimensions are low frequency and all the h[eight] dimensions are high frequency. So they basically interleave them', so 'all the axes are exposed to both low and high frequency'. His hedged direction (temporal low, height high) is the reverse of what standard RoPE's ordering gives a [t ... w ... h] layout, where the first block gets the highest frequencies; the KP does not depend on which axis gets which end (this thread's check; recorded, not imported). Spoken evidence: timestamps: before, time was 'implicit in the positional encodings', each frame getting a notion of time only from its position; now a token stands for each time, 'helpful presumably because ... you can directly refer to, like what happened after two seconds' (55:19-55:59); RoPE recap: the inner product depends only on the distance (51:17-51:29). Flag (15:40-16:13): in the CLIP Q&A he says 1D position ids reportedly do about as well as a 2D variant 'for classification', so the first misconception was restated (2026-10-02) to the false extension: that 1D positions are also enough at Qwen2-VL's dynamic resolution.

prerequisites.note: Variable-resolution grids (L219-L220) are why a 2D/3D position scheme is needed; MRoPE follows at L223.

external_prerequisites.note: RoPE and its per-dimension frequency bands were taught in lecture 3; MRoPE partitions those dimensions across axes.

misconceptions.belief: Since 1D raster positions work for a fixed-size ViT classifier, they are also enough for Qwen2-VL's dynamic-resolution images.
misconceptions.why_wrong: With a fixed grid the model can learn which 1D offset means 'directly below', which is why 1D positions do about as well for classification (the professor, 15:40-16:13: 'for classification, maybe it doesn't matter'). Under dynamic resolution the row length, and so that offset, changes from image to image, and video adds time as a third axis; MRoPE gives time, height and width their own axes (L246) so 2D adjacency is explicit at any resolution.

misconceptions.belief: In the blocked layout [t t t t w w w w h h h h] each axis already sees the full range of rotary frequencies.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A contiguous block of dimensions covers a contiguous band of frequencies, so one axis gets only high-frequency dimensions and another only low-frequency ones; interleaving [t w h t w h ...] is what 'distribute all axes ... to low- and high-frequency bands' (L246) means.

misconceptions.belief: The temporal position id tells the model how much time passed between frames.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Temporal ids count sampled frames, not seconds; two clips sampled at different frame rates get the same ids. That is why Qwen3-VL adds explicit timestamp tokens (L248).

predict.q: Qwen3-VL switches from the blocked MRoPE layout [t t t t w w w w h h h h] to the interleaved [t w h t w h t w h t w h]. What changes for each axis?
choices: each axis now gets dimensions in both the low- and the high-frequency bands
each axis gets more rotary dimensions in total
the temporal axis gets more dimensions than width or height
predict.answer: each axis now gets dimensions in both the low- and the high-frequency bands
predict.why: L246: 'distribute all axes (temporal, width, height) to low- and high-frequency bands'. The number of dimensions per axis is the same (four each in the schematic); only their placement along the frequency spectrum changes.
predict.targets_misconception: In the blocked layout [t t t t w w w w h h h h] each axis already sees the full range of rotary frequencies.
predict.distractor_from: more dimensions in total: misreading interleaving as adding capacity; temporal gets more: assuming time is privileged (the schematic at L247 keeps axes equal)

transfer.q: Video A is sampled at 2 frames per second, video B at 0.5 frames per second; both yield 40 frames. Under MRoPE temporal position ids alone, what does the model know about the elapsed time covered by each video, and what does Qwen3-VL's explicit timestamp token add?
transfer.answer: Nothing that distinguishes them: both get temporal ids 0..39, so a 20-second clip and an 80-second clip look identical in position space; the timestamp tokens inject the absolute time of each frame into the sequence so the model can tell 20 s from 80 s and reason about rates.
transfer.why: Temporal ids index frames; L248 adds 'explicit video timestamps (as separate tokens rather in positional embeddings)' precisely because the position embedding cannot carry sampling rate.
transfer.varies: frame sampling rate (2 fps vs 0.5 fps) with frame count held equal as the misleading cue
transfer.invariant: position ids count sampled frames, not seconds

check.q: A Qwen3-VL user asks how many seconds pass between two events in a video. Which ingredient of Qwen3-VL carries that information to the model?
choices: the explicit timestamp tokens added for video
the temporal axis of the MRoPE position ids alone
the width and height axes of the MRoPE ids
the interleaved [t w h] frequency layout
check.answer: the explicit timestamp tokens added for video
check.why: L246-L248: Qwen3-VL adds explicit video timestamps as tokens. Temporal position ids count frames, not seconds, so clips sampled at different rates look alike; the interleaving only spreads axes over frequency bands.
check.varies: asks which component carries elapsed time instead of comparing two sampling rates
check.invariant: MRoPE temporal ids index frames; absolute time comes from the timestamp tokens
check.targets_misconception: The temporal position id tells the model how much time passed between frames.
distractor_from: 'the temporal axis of the MRoPE position ids alone' <- misconception: 'The temporal position id tells the model how much time passed between frames.'
'the width and height axes of the MRoPE ids' <- plausible: confuses spatial axes with time
'the interleaved [t w h] frequency layout' <- plausible: confuses how the axes are spread over frequency bands with where elapsed time is encoded

retrieval.q: Why does Qwen3-VL interleave the t, w, h axes across MRoPE's rotary dimensions instead of giving each axis its own contiguous block?
retrieval.answer: So that every axis gets both low- and high-frequency dimensions.

retrieval.q: Write the interleaved MRoPE dimension pattern the lecture contrasts with the blocked one.
retrieval.answer: [t w h t w h t w h t w h] rather than [t t t t w w w w h h h h].

retrieval.q: How does Qwen3-VL convey video timestamps?
retrieval.answer: As explicit separate tokens, not through the positional embedding.

prompts.self_explain: Why would giving the height axis only slowly rotating (low-frequency) dimensions hurt the model's ability to tell adjacent rows apart?

presentations.notice: listen for: why interleave: a blocked layout gives each axis only low or only high frequencies

Switch from blocked to interleaved. Each axis still owns 4 of the 12 slots, but height's slots go from only the slowest (8–11) to a spread from 2 to 11. Then give clips A and B different frame rates with the same frame count: their temporal ids are identical while the seconds differ, until the timestamp tokens are switched on.

knowledge_points.label: Chameleon: VQ-VAE discrete image tokens let one autoregressive model read and generate images
knowledge_points.statement: Continuous-encoder VLMs can analyse images but cannot generate them (that needs a diffusion model); Chameleon instead quantises images with a VQ-VAE (encode to codebook indices, decode back, minimise reconstruction loss) so a 512x512 image becomes 1024 tokens from an 8192-entry codebook (a 32x32 grid, 16x16 pixels and 13 bits per token, this thread's arithmetic), trains a new BPE tokenizer over text plus image codes, and models everything autoregressively, at the cost that discretisation loses information (OCR suffers).

anchors.quote: So far: VLMs encode images (via CLIP or SigLIP), inject into LM ... Disadvantage: can't generate images (need diffusion) ... Chameleon: map everything into discrete tokens ... Advantage: can analyze and generate images in a uniform way

Key difference: encoder needs to map to discrete tokens (so we can generate them) ... VQ-VAE (Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder) ... Idea: map image to a discrete codebook, decode back to image and minimize reconstruction loss
Encodes 512 x 512 image into 1024 tokens (codebook of size 8192) ... Train a new BPE tokenizer
Elegant (just autoregressive modeling of discrete tokens) ... Not as performant (discretization loses information - think OCR)
Continuous encoders + Transformer + diffusion models for generation

anchors.ref: Chameleon overview and example figures (chameleon.png, chameleon-example.png, shown at L276-L277); image tokenizer §2.1

anchors.quote: So first of all, these models don't generate videos or images. ... All the multimodal stuff is on the input side. ... You're always generating text.

So, so far, VLMs encode images into these vectors and then they inject them into a language model. ... You can also attach a diffusion head. ... This is appealing because now you can analyze and generate images in the same way.

which is called vector quantized variational autoencoder. ... And this gets rounded to the nearest code. ... So you have a codebook which has, let's say, 8,000 codes. ... And then you train these VQ-VAEs by basically minimizing the reconstruction loss.

you have 512 by 512 images that are converted into 1,024 tokens, and each token comes from a vocabulary of 8,000. ... They train a new tokenizer because now you have different-- your data looks different than if it were just normal natural language.
This is just normal language model training. ... There's no adapter. ... There's just a language model now.

But the downside is that it turned out this model was not really as performant, and the discretization does definitely lose its information. ... Again, if you discretize very small print, you're not going to be able to read it anymore.

So VQ-VAEs were popular for a while. ... Well, you have to generate discrete things and you basically put all your data into this discrete form. ... But then diffusion models came out and became popular and viable for generation.

provenance.filtering_note: 1024 tokens for 512x512 is a 32x32 grid, so each token summarises a 16x16-pixel cell with log2(8192) = 13 bits; 1024 x 13 bits is about 1.7 kB against 786 kB of raw 8-bit RGB, a ~470x compression: all this thread's arithmetic on L284, offered as the reason 'discretization loses information' (L297). The VQ-VAE commitment loss, straight-through estimator and codebook update are not in the lecture; vq-vae.png (L283) is the paper's figure. Make-A-Scene (L279) is linked under 'Vision encoder' without a sentence. 'Train a new BPE tokenizer' (L285) is one line: the text vocabulary is retrained and the 8192 image codes are added. The summary's 'Continuous encoders + Transformer + diffusion models for generation' (L45) is the professor's view of the current recipe; the lecture shows no diffusion mechanism. Spoken evidence: the continuous VLMs 'don't generate videos or images. All the multimodal stuff is on the input side' (Q&A 1:00:02-1:00:09); besides Chameleon, one can 'attach a diffusion head' to a VLM (1:07:55); discrete tokens appeal because analysis and generation work 'in the same way' ('maybe this reflects that I'm a language person', 1:08:10-1:08:23); the VQ-VAE is described as encode to a continuous vector, round to the nearest of about 8,000 codes, decode, minimize reconstruction loss, with the extra terms needed for the non-differentiable rounding skipped (1:09:41-1:10:46); a new tokenizer because the data 'looks different' (1:11:12); training is 'just normal language model training ... no adapter' (1:11:24-1:11:39); Chameleon's results are not shown (1:13:16); history: VQ tokens let a Transformer generate images by emitting discrete symbols, until diffusion models became viable, so the approach is 'less popular than it used to be' (1:14:05-1:14:35). In the summary he speculates that closed frontier models pair a continuous encoder with diffusion for generation, 'but that's my speculation' (1:15:14-1:15:31). '8,000' (1:10:00, 1:10:46) rounds L284's 8192.

prerequisites.note: Chameleon is the literal version of 'convert everything into tokens' with discrete tokens (L17-L18, L274).
Defined by contrast with the continuous-injection template (L271-L272).
Both encoders lose detail for different reasons: CLIP by objective and crop, VQ-VAE by quantisation; OCR is the lecture's test case in both (L160, L297).

external_prerequisites.note: 'Train a new BPE tokenizer' (L285) assumes BPE from lecture 1.
Adding 8192 image codes to the vocabulary and spending 1024 tokens per image is the same vocabulary/length trade.

misconceptions.belief: A LLaVA-style model could generate images if you just trained it longer, since it already understands them.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Its image path is a continuous encoder feeding the LM (L271); the LM's output is a distribution over text tokens and the CLIP features have no decoder, so 'can't generate images (need diffusion)' (L272). Generation needs tokens that can be emitted and decoded, which is why Chameleon's encoder 'needs to map to discrete tokens' (L280).

misconceptions.belief: Discretising images into tokens makes them 'just like text' with no loss.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each of the 1024 tokens stands for a 16x16-pixel cell with one of 8192 codes (L284); fine detail below that granularity is gone, which the lecture flags as 'discretization loses information - think OCR' (L297).

predict.q: Why can a CLIP-plus-projector VLM like LLaVA not produce an image, according to the lecture?
choices: its LM emits only text tokens, and the continuous visual features have no decoder
it uses too few visual tokens per image to describe every pixel
its projector is a single linear layer, too weak to map back to pixels
it was never trained to generate; more training on images would fix it
predict.answer: its LM emits only text tokens, and the continuous visual features have no decoder
predict.why: its visual path is a continuous encoder feeding the LM and the LM emits text tokens; there is nothing to decode into pixels. L271-L272: encode and inject, 'can't generate images (need diffusion)'. Chameleon fixes this by making the encoder produce discrete tokens 'so we can generate them' (L280) and decoding them with the VQ-VAE decoder (L282).

'linear projector too weak' <- plausible: misreads 'Flamingo and Q-former are more complex' (L139) as the generation bottleneck

transfer.q: A team wants a Chameleon-style model to read 512x512 scans of receipts in 6-point type. Before any numbers, say what kind of failure the lecture predicts and why; then use the tokenizer's figures (1024 tokens, codebook 8192) to say how large a pixel cell each token must summarise.
transfer.answer: Small text will be misread or lost: discretisation throws away fine detail ('think OCR'), because the whole image must be expressed as a fixed number of codebook choices; 1024 tokens on 512x512 is a 32x32 grid, so each token summarises a 16x16-pixel cell with one of 8192 codes, and 6-point glyphs are smaller than that cell.
transfer.why: L297 names the failure and its cause; L284 gives the numbers; the cell size follows from 512/sqrt(1024) = 16 (this thread's arithmetic).
transfer.varies: task domain: dense small text (OCR) instead of natural images
transfer.invariant: a fixed token grid and finite codebook bound the detail any image can carry

check.q: A VQ-VAE turns a 256x256 RGB image (8 bits per channel) into a 16x16 grid of tokens from a 16,384-entry codebook. By what factor is the token sequence smaller than the raw pixels, counted in bits?
check.why: Raw: 256 x 256 x 3 x 8 = 1,572,864 bits. Tokens: 16 x 16 = 256 tokens of log2(16,384) = 14 bits = 3,584 bits. Ratio ≈ 439. Discretisation must throw information away, which is why the lecture says OCR suffers (L296-L297).
check.varies: a different tokenizer (256 tokens, 16K codebook) and asks the compression ratio instead of the pixel cell size
check.invariant: a fixed number of codebook choices carries far fewer bits than the pixels, so discretisation is lossy
check.targets_misconception: Discretising images into tokens makes them 'just like text' with no loss.

retrieval.q: What is the lecture's stated disadvantage of CLIP/SigLIP-based VLMs?
retrieval.answer: They cannot generate images; that needs diffusion.

retrieval.q: State the VQ-VAE idea.
retrieval.answer: Map the image to a discrete codebook, decode back to an image, and minimise reconstruction loss.

retrieval.q: How many tokens does Chameleon's tokenizer produce for a 512x512 image, with what codebook size?
retrieval.answer: 1024 tokens; codebook of size 8192.

retrieval.q: What are the lecture's one-word verdicts on Chameleon's design and its performance?
retrieval.answer: Elegant (pure autoregressive modeling of discrete tokens); not as performant (discretisation loses information, e.g. OCR).

In VQ mode the readout sets the raw pixel bits against the token bits. At 512 px with 16-px cells and 8192 codes, 1024 tokens of 13 bits stand in for about 6.3 million bits (about 470× smaller), and each token must summarise a whole 16 × 16-pixel cell.

knowledge_points.label: Mixing modalities: balance long low-density visual data against text and watch for norm growth
knowledge_points.statement: Visual and text tokens differ in information density and entropy, so a mixed model must rebalance them: Qwen3-VL uses a square-root-normalized per-token loss so long video examples do not dominate text, and Chameleon found that low-entropy text tokens next to high-entropy image tokens cause norm growth and logit drift, fixed with QK-norm and z-loss.

anchors.quote: Square-root-normalized per-token loss: balance text and multimodal data (video examples are long, don't want to dominate)
Text tokens have low entropy, image tokens have high entropy, leads to norm growth, logit drift problem ... Fixes: QK norm, z-loss regularization
Balance images + video (lower information density) and text for training stability
Training with multiple modalities is tricky

anchors.ref: Chameleon §3.1 training stability (norm growth, QK-norm, z-loss), L292-L293

anchors.quote: And this would mean that the video examples are going to dominate. ... the details aren't too clear. ... But I believe they normalized each example by the square root of the length to basically downweight the impact of really long examples.

So the videos and images can have more-- especially video have more tokens. ... We talked in the last or two weeks ago about data mixtures. ... I wouldn't say that the number of multimodal tokens vastly outnumbers text tokens.

So just calling things discrete tokens isn't hiding the fact that there's an image living there. ... Most words are predictable, whereas image tokens have very high entropy. ... I don't know what shade of blue this exact token is going to be.

And so as a result, they found that training with this mixture led to a lot of the norms of the parameters to grow and to generate loss instability. ... They were able to mitigate or fix this to some extent via QK norm and z-loss regularization, which controls the norm growth.

I think, in general, when you're dealing with multiple modalities, you have to think carefully about weighing them properly. ... For example, video certainly has lower information density than text. ... So you don't want a video to overwhelm your text.

provenance.filtering_note: The lecture does not define 'square-root-normalized' (L249). A plain per-token mean over the batch weights an example in proportion to its token count (so an 8000-token video outweighs a 500-token text 16:1); a per-example mean weights them equally; dividing each example's summed loss by the square root of its token count sits between the two. That reading is this thread's; the Qwen3-VL report has the definition and the predict prompt below only uses the two lecture-grounded extremes. Chameleon's diagnosis (L292) is one sentence: why low-entropy tokens next to high-entropy ones drive norm growth is not explained here; the paper attributes it to softmax translation invariance letting logits drift when modalities compete. QK-norm and z-loss are named, not re-derived (lecture 3 has them). Correction, hedged (56:29-56:41): the note says the lecture does not define 'square-root-normalized' and that the between-the-extremes reading is this thread's. Aloud: 'the details aren't too clear. But I believe they normalized each example by the square root of the length to basically downweight the impact of really long examples', which is this thread's reading; the report's exact formula is still not given. Spoken evidence: the entropy contrast is made concrete, 'Most words are predictable', while for an image token 'I don't know what shade of blue this exact token is going to be' (1:12:33-1:12:46); 'just calling things discrete tokens isn't hiding the fact that there's an image living there' (1:12:25); the instability is growth of 'the norms of the parameters' with loss instability, controlled 'to some extent' by QK-norm and z-loss (1:12:50-1:13:16). There is still no mechanism for why the entropy gap drives norm growth. Q&A (1:02:03-1:02:56): long video is one reason for the normalization; any source can be down-weighted as in the data-mixture lecture (lecture 14); multimodal tokens do not 'vastly' outnumber the tens of trillions of text tokens. Summary: video has 'lower information density than text', so it must not 'overwhelm your text' (1:16:20-1:16:41).

prerequisites.note: The stability problem (L291-L293) is stated for Chameleon's all-discrete token stream, where text and image tokens share one softmax.
Video examples are long (L249) because tokens scale with frames x area (L221).

Named as a fix at L293; lecture 3 explains it keeps the softmax normaliser near 1, which is what 'logit drift' violates.

misconceptions.belief: Averaging the loss over all tokens in a batch treats each training example equally.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A per-token mean weights each example by its token count, so long video examples dominate (L249: 'video examples are long, don't want to dominate'); that is why Qwen3-VL changes the normalisation.

misconceptions.belief: Image tokens are harder to predict, so they should get more weight to be learned.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The lecture's concern runs the other way: high-entropy image tokens already dominate the loss and destabilise training (norm growth, logit drift, L292); the fixes constrain logits (QK-norm, z-loss, L293) and the balance goal is to keep text from being drowned (L44).

predict.q: A batch holds one 500-token text example and one 8000-token video example. Under an ordinary per-token mean loss, roughly what fraction of the loss (and so of the gradient) comes from the video?
choices: about 94% (8000 of 8500 tokens)
about 50% (one example each)
about 6% (image tokens are down-weighted)
predict.why: A per-token mean sums every token's loss and divides by 8500, so the video contributes 8000/8500 = 0.94; this is the domination L249 refers to and the reason for re-normalising.
predict.targets_misconception: Averaging the loss over all tokens in a batch treats each training example equally.
predict.distractor_from: 50%: 'per-token averaging treats examples equally'; 6%: 'image tokens should be down/up-weighted by difficulty' (inverted)

transfer.q: A team adds 30% raw audio tokens (from a high-entropy codec) to a text LM's pretraining stream in one shared vocabulary. Using Chameleon's analysis, predict which training symptom to watch for, name its stated cause, and list the two architectural fixes to install before the run.
transfer.answer: Watch for norm growth and logit drift; the cause is mixing low-entropy text tokens with high-entropy (audio) tokens in one autoregressive softmax; install QK-norm and z-loss regularisation.
transfer.why: L292-L293 give cause and fixes for the image case; the mechanism depends on entropy mismatch, not on the modality being visual.
transfer.varies: modality (audio codec tokens instead of VQ image tokens), modality dimension
transfer.invariant: high-entropy discrete tokens sharing a softmax with low-entropy text

check.q: In a mixed text-and-video model, long video examples are dominating the gradient over short text examples. Which fix named in the lecture targets this problem?
choices: QK-norm in every attention layer
a square-root-normalized per-token loss
z-loss regularisation on the logits
extra loss weight on the harder image tokens
check.why: L249: Qwen3-VL uses a square-root-normalized per-token loss to balance text and multimodal data so long video examples do not dominate. QK-norm and z-loss (L292-L293) fix Chameleon's norm growth and logit drift, a different problem.
check.varies: the symptom is example-length imbalance (Qwen3-VL) rather than entropy-driven instability (Chameleon)
check.invariant: text and visual tokens differ in density and entropy, and each imbalance has its own fix
check.targets_misconception: Averaging the loss over all tokens in a batch treats each training example equally.
distractor_from: 'QK-norm in every attention layer' <- plausible: applies Chameleon's stability fix to the length-imbalance problem
'z-loss regularisation on the logits' <- plausible: applies Chameleon's stability fix to the length-imbalance problem
'extra loss weight on the harder image tokens' <- misconception: 'Image tokens are harder to predict, so they should get more weight to be learned.'

retrieval.q: Why does Qwen3-VL use a square-root-normalized per-token loss?
retrieval.answer: To balance text and multimodal data, because long video examples would otherwise dominate.

retrieval.q: What entropy difference does the lecture blame for Chameleon's instability, and what two symptoms does it cause?
retrieval.answer: Text tokens have low entropy and image tokens high entropy; this leads to norm growth and logit drift.

retrieval.q: Name Chameleon's two stability fixes.
retrieval.answer: QK-norm and z-loss regularisation.

Under the per-token mean the video's share is its token count divided by all the batch's tokens, so it takes over as the video grows. The per-example row and the square-root row (the square-root row is this thread's reading of L249) both shrink that share.
